lines.text:
Ready for Anything — Inside the First Aid Room

Every school, workplace, and sports club has a first aid room — a small, clean space where injuries and minor medical problems are treated before a doctor or ambulance arrives. Knowing the vocabulary of first aid could one day help you help someone.

The first aid kit is the most important item in the room. It contains everything needed for basic treatment. A bandage wraps around a wound to protect it and stop bleeding. Gauze — a thin, breathable fabric — covers the wound underneath. A gauze pad is placed directly over the injury. Adhesive tape holds the gauze in place. An antiseptic wipe cleans the wound and kills bacteria. Scissors cut bandages and tape. Tweezers remove splinters or small objects. A safety pin fastens bandages. An elastic bandage wraps around sprains and strains. A triangular bandage makes a sling for an injured arm.

For different types of injuries, the kit includes specific items. Burn cream soothes burns. A cold pack or ice pack reduces swelling. A heat pack or hot pack relaxes tight muscles. A finger splint keeps a broken or jammed finger straight. Medical tape is stronger than adhesive tape. Antibiotic ointment prevents infection. Hydrocortisone cream treats itching and rashes. A plaster — known as a 'Band-Aid' in American English — covers small cuts. A butterfly strip pulls the edges of a cut together.

For more serious situations, the first aid room has larger equipment. A stretcher carries an injured person who cannot walk. A wheelchair moves someone who can sit but not stand. A crutch helps someone walk with a leg injury. A splint immobilises a broken bone. A neck brace supports the head and neck after a spinal injury.

Medical monitoring equipment is also available. A stethoscope listens to the heart and lungs. A thermometer measures body temperature. A pulse oximeter clips onto the finger and measures oxygen levels in the blood. A blood pressure cuff wraps around the upper arm. A blood glucose monitor checks blood sugar levels. A penlight shines into the eyes to check for concussion. A tongue depressor helps examine the throat.

In a life-threatening emergency, two pieces of equipment can save lives. A CPR mask allows someone to give rescue breaths safely during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. An AED — automated external defibrillator — delivers an electric shock to restart a heart that has stopped. A first aid manual provides step-by-step instructions for every situation.

Wound care supplies include saline solution for cleaning wounds, hydrogen peroxide as a disinfectant, iodine for deeper wounds, cotton swabs for applying ointment, sterile gloves to prevent infection, a syringe for irrigating wounds, a suture kit for stitching (used by trained personnel only), wound closure strips, a wound dressing for larger injuries, a skin stapler for emergency wound closure, and an irrigation syringe for flushing debris from wounds.

The first aid room is quiet most of the time. But when an accident happens, everything in that room — and the knowledge to use it — can make the difference between a minor incident and a serious emergency.

lines.text: First Aid at Work — Legal Requirements
lines.name: First Aid at Work — Legal Requirements

lines.text: In many countries, workplaces are legally required to have a trained first aider and a stocked first aid kit. The UK requires one per 50 employees; regulations vary elsewhere.
lines.name: In many countries, workplaces are legally required to have a trained first aider and a stocked first aid kit. The UK requires one per 50 employees; regulations vary elsewhere.

lines.text: Different countries have different emergency numbers: 911 (USA/Canada), 999 (UK), 112 (EU/International), 000 (Australia). Teaching the local number is essential.

lines.text: Medicine Cabinet vs First Aid Kit
lines.name: Medicine Cabinet vs First Aid Kit

lines.text: A "medicine cabinet" is typically found in bathrooms at home. A "first aid kit" is the portable box used in workplaces and schools. Don't confuse them — first aid kits should NOT contain prescription medicines.
lines.name: A "medicine cabinet" is typically found in bathrooms at home. A "first aid kit" is the portable box used in workplaces and schools. Don't confuse them — first aid kits should NOT contain prescription medicines.

lines.text: "Wound" is more formal/medical than "cut" or "scrape". In casual speech: "I got a cut on my finger." In a report: "The patient presented with a superficial wound to the index finger."

lines.name: ❌ "He has broken his leg. We need to call an ambulance immediately." — Is this correct?

lines.text: A reassurance point: 'He has broken his leg' (present perfect) and 'He broke his leg' (past simple) are both correct here. Present perfect emphasises the current result (his leg is broken now). Past simple focuses on the event. Both are natural in an emergency. Don't second-guess a correct sentence.

lines.text: 'Feel' is a linking verb — use an adjective, not an adverb. 'I feel bad' (adjective — describes your state). 'I feel badly' means your sense of touch doesn't work well. Same rule: 'I feel sick' (not *sickly), 'I feel tired' (not *tiredly), 'I feel happy' (not *happily).

lines.text: 'Lie – lay – lain' (no object, intransitive): 'She lies down. She lay down yesterday. She has lain there for an hour.' 'Lay – laid – laid' (with object, transitive): 'Lay the patient on the stretcher. He laid the bandage on the table.' The past tense of 'lie' is 'lay' — which looks like the present tense of a different verb.

lines.text: 'Information' is uncountable — no plural 's' and no 'a.' 'Some information', 'a piece of information', 'useful information.' Never 'informations.' Other uncountable nouns: 'advice', 'knowledge', 'equipment', 'furniture', 'luggage.'
